paper_a.title: State-independent proof of Kochen-Specker theorem with 13 rays

paper_b.title: State Independent Proof of Kochen-Specker Theorem with Thirty Rank-Two Projectors

metadata.description: Both papers establish the Kochen-Specker no-go theorem via state-independent finite constructions, but with fundamentally different witness sets and proof strategies. Paper A (Yu-Oh) works in the qutrit (3-dim) Hilbert space with 13 rays organised on a magic cube and proves the contradiction either via a direct value-assignment lemma or via a state-independent KS inequality with operator identity L = 25/3 I. Paper B (Toh) works in the three-qubit (8-dim) space with 30 rank-2 projectors derived from the Mermin pentagram / Kernaghan-Peres 40-ray system and proves a parity contradiction (even left-hand sum vs. odd 15 right-hand sum). They share the target theorem and the NCHV/sum/product-rule axiomatic frame but differ in dimension, witness set, and proof technique, making this an alternative-proof (AP) pair.

matches.explanation: Both papers cite the identical Kochen-Specker theorem as the target no-go statement: NCHV theories cannot reproduce QM in dimension > 2 (paper A) / >= 3 (paper B). Both list Kochen & Specker 1967 as origin and both treat it as the external statement they will give a state-independent proof of.

Both define a noncontextual hidden-variable model: each observable carries a pre-determined value independent of the measurement context. Paper A frames it via the HV measure rho_lambda; paper B uses the value function v(.). Same mathematical object.
Both define a measurement context as a maximal set of mutually compatible (commuting) observables. Wording is essentially identical.

Paper A bundles the product rule and the sum rule into a single definition (DP410.3). Paper B separates them as two assumptions: AssumP412.1 (product rule v(L)v(M)=v(N) for commuting LM=N) and AssumP412.2 (sum rule v(L)+v(M)=v(N) for commuting L+M=N). The mathematical content matches one-to-one.

Paper A's AssumP410.1 lists the two KS-assignment conditions (basis-independence of {0,1} ray values; exactly one ray = 1 per orthonormal basis). Paper B's DP412.5 expresses the same value-function rule v(P_i) in {0,1} for projectors (plus +/-1 for Mermin observables). The conditions encode the same KS-style value rule on rank-1 projectors.

Both define a value assignment to projectors. Paper A's KS value assignment is the canonical {0,1} rule on rays of any Hilbert space, with the two basis conditions; paper B's value function v(.) extends to rank-2 projectors and to +/-1-valued Mermin observables. The roles match (the central object that the proof shows cannot exist consistently) but B's version is broader because it must accommodate sum-rule arguments on planes.

Both papers pose the same minimisation problem -- find a state-independent KS test using as few witnesses as possible -- but on different systems. Paper A targets the qutrit (minimising number of rays); paper B targets the three-qubit system (minimising number of projectors, allowing rank-2). Same conceptual problem statement, different ambient dimension.

These are the two papers' respective concrete witness sets. Paper A: the 13 qutrit rays {y_k^+/-, h_alpha, z_k} from the magic-cube construction (DP410.6 + the explicit list in EP410.1). Paper B: the 40 Kernaghan-Peres rays in R^8 (ExP412.1) with the 15 rank-1 completeness relations (EP412.2). Both serve the same role -- the explicit finite ray system on which the KS contradiction is exhibited -- but live in different dimensions and have different cardinalities. This is the central locus of the AP relationship.

Both encode operator-level identities/completeness that drive the contradiction. Paper A: the operator-sum identities sum y = 2I, sum h = 4/3 I, sum z = I, which yield the QM expectation 25/3 (or 4/3 for the original-rule version). Paper B: 15 rank-2 completeness relations sum P_{i,j} = I with each of 30 planes appearing exactly twice. They play parallel structural roles -- rewriting the witness system as identities on the identity operator from which the value-rule contradiction is read off -- but the algebraic mechanism differs (operator-sum identity vs. parity counting on a multi-set of completeness relations).

These are the two papers' main state-independent KS results. Paper A's TP410.4 (original-rule version): a 13-ray construction yielding sum_alpha <h_alpha>_c <= 1 classically vs. 4/3 quantumly. Paper B's TP412.5: a 30-projector construction in R^8 yielding a parity contradiction between the even left-hand sum and the odd 15 on the right. Both are the headline state-independent KS proofs; they share the conclusion 'no NCHV assignment exists for this finite witness set' but differ in dimension (3 vs 8), in witness type (rays vs rank-2 projectors), and in proof mechanism (algebraic identity vs parity).

Paper A's TP410.6 is the magic-cube state-independent KS inequality: a noncontextuality inequality bounded classically by 8 and quantumly by 25/3, violated by every qutrit state. Paper B's TP412.5 plays the analogous role at the 8-dim level. Paper A's RP412.2 explicitly notes that B's 30-projector proof can be cast as a Cabello-style noncontextuality inequality, supporting the analogy. Distinct in math content (continuous bound vs. parity) but parallel in the structural role of 'state-independent KS inequality saturated by all states of the relevant system'.

Cluster correspondence between the two papers' main proofs. Paper A's PP410.3 derives the original-rule KS inequality by integrating the at-most-one-h_alpha bound against rho_lambda and comparing to the QM value 4/3 obtained from the operator identity; PP410.5 derives the magic-cube operator identity L = 25/3 I from edge counts and adjacency-orthogonality. Paper B's PP412.1 derives the 30-projector contradiction by parity counting (each of 30 planes appears twice, so the LHS is even, while RHS = 15 is odd). Both are the central proof modules; their inner step DAGs differ in interesting ways (algebraic identity-chasing in A vs. parity counting in B), which is the essence of the alternative-proof relationship -- see the L2 step matches below.

Composite L2 cluster justified by the parent match (PP410.5 ~ PP412.1) above. Both proof step chains start by expanding/constructing the operator object (PSP410.9 expands L in r_v ; PSP412.1 builds rank-2 completeness from rank-1), then apply edge / multiplicity counts (PSP410.10 uses 24 edges + degree counts ; PSP412.3 uses 'each plane appears twice'), then conclude the algebraic identity / parity contradiction (PSP410.11 derives L = 25/3 I ; PSP412.5 derives the even-vs-odd contradiction). The step-level mathematics differs sharply (algebraic operator identity vs. parity bookkeeping), which is exactly the AP signal we'd expect.

Paper A's uniqueness theorem -- that the 13 magic-cube rays are determined uniquely (up to a global unitary) by the orthogonality graph Delta_13 -- has no counterpart in paper B. Paper B never claims uniqueness for its 30-projector configuration; on the contrary, PrP412.1 emphasises that 243 distinct rank-2 proofs can be constructed from the 40-ray completeness structure.

The 'at most one h_alpha = 1' lemma is a paper-A-specific structural fact about the 13-ray graph used by the original-rule proof. Paper B's parity-based proof never argues a per-context value lemma of this kind.

Paper A's combinatorial inequality on Delta_13 (sum a_v - 1/4 sum Gamma_uv a_u a_v <= 8 over +/-1 assignments) is the classical-side bound for the magic-cube inequality. Paper B has no analogue: its classical bound arises from parity, not a continuous combinatorial inequality.

The operator identity L = 25/3 I (paper A) is the QM-side computation that gives the magic-cube inequality its state-independent character. Paper B has no scalar-multiple-of-identity calculation; its quantum side is the trivial sum P_{i,j} = I per context.
The qutrit ray triple-representation r = (a,b,c) is paper-A-specific notation tied to the 3-dim setting. Paper B's R^8 construction has no analogue at this level.

Paper A's orthogonality graph Delta_13 (13 vertices, adjacency matrix Gamma) is central to its inequality and proof. Paper B mentions a 30-vertex hypergraph (RP412.1) for its planes, but RP412.1 is auxiliary and structurally different (hypergraph rather than simple orthogonality graph; carries no analogous adjacency-matrix role in the proof).

Paper A's dichotomic observables A_v = I - 2 r_v (eigenvalues +/-1) are introduced specifically for the magic-cube inequality's correlation form. Paper B's analogue would be the projectors P_{i,j} themselves (already covered above) -- there is no separate dichotomic-observable construction.
Paper A's original-rule KS inequality sum_alpha <h_alpha>_c <= 1 is the headline scalar inequality of the original-rule proof, with no direct counterpart in paper B's parity argument.

Paper A's magic-cube inequality in operator form (LHS <= 8) is the scalar witness of the state-independent inequality. Paper B's witness is a parity statement, not a numerical inequality, so there is no direct equation-level analogue.
Proof of uniqueness of the 13-ray realisation (parent TP410.2 unmatched). No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of the at-most-one-h_alpha lemma (parent TP410.3 unmatched). No counterpart in paper B's parity-based proof.
The proof of the combinatorial inequality on Delta_13 (case analysis on t in {0,...,6}) is paper-A-specific; paper B's classical bound is parity-based and admits no such case enumeration.

Paper A conjectures 13 is the minimal ray count for a state-independent KS proof on the qutrit. Paper B makes a parallel-but-distinct minimality claim (RP412.3) for the 8-dim Mermin-pentagram setting at 30 projectors -- different system, different witness type, so we do not align these as the same claim.
The Mermin pentagram (ten three-qubit observables in five contexts) is the organising object of paper B's construction and has no qutrit analogue in paper A.

The rank-1 vs rank-2 projector dichotomy (rays vs planes) is central to paper B's contribution -- using rank-2 projectors to reduce the witness count from 36/40 to 30. Paper A works only with rank-1 rays, so this distinction has no counterpart.
The five Mermin pentagram product relations are paper-B-specific; paper A's witness equations are completely different (the explicit ray triples in EP410.1).

Paper B's enumeration result -- 243 distinct rank-2 KS proofs derivable from the 40-ray completeness structure -- is paper-B-specific. Paper A explicitly proves uniqueness of its construction (TP410.2), the structural opposite, which we do not treat as the same node.

Paper B's minimality claim (30 projectors beats the rank-1 records of 36/38/40 in the Mermin-pentagram R^8 setting) is system-specific; paper A's analogous minimality conjecture (ClP410.1) is for the qutrit at 13 rays -- different system, so we keep them separate.
